fields.security_summary: DDR3 SDRAM as defined in JESD79-3C is a commodity memory device with NO confidentiality, NO authentication, NO bus-level encryption, NO access control, NO secure erase, NO replay protection. The base protocol provides only data-integrity protection via single-bit parity / ECC at the system level (optional, requires +8 ECC DRAM per rank). All security functionality — at-rest encryption, anti-replay, key management, secure boot — is layered above the DDR3 channel by the memory controller / SoC / operating system (e.g., AMD SME, Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone-aware controllers, Apple A-series memory protection).

security_features_at_protocol_level.name: System-level ECC (SEC-DED)
security_features_at_protocol_level.scope: Per 64-bit data word; requires an additional ×8 ECC DRAM per rank.
security_features_at_protocol_level.description: Single-Error Correcting, Double-Error Detecting Hamming code; controller-side encode/decode. JEDEC ECC DIMM modules expose +8 ECC bits per 64-bit word. NOT a cryptographic MAC.

security_features_at_protocol_level.name: Permanent Write Protect (none)
security_features_at_protocol_level.description: DDR3 has no built-in write protect register. All cells are writable as long as the addressed bank is open.

fields.no_confidentiality: The DDR3 bus carries plaintext data on the DQ lines. An attacker with physical bus access (probe / interposer) can sniff all reads and writes in plain. Cold-boot attacks (recovering DRAM cell contents after power-off with rapid chilling and re-power) are well-documented against unprotected DDR3.
fields.no_authentication: DDR3 has no command authentication. A rogue device on the bus or a tampered controller can issue any command (including SRE, ZQCL, MRS to alter Mode Registers).
fields.no_access_control: DDR3 has no per-bank, per-row, or per-address access control. Every command is accepted unconditionally per the Command Truth Table.
fields.rowhammer_class_vulnerabilities: DDR3 is the first DRAM generation where the Rowhammer side-channel was experimentally demonstrated (Kim et al. 2014). Repeatedly activating a 'hammer' row causes adjacent rows' cells to leak charge faster than tREFI can replenish, producing bit flips. JESD79-3C does not specify any Rowhammer defense; later JEDEC standards (DDR4, DDR5) added Targeted Row Refresh (TRR) and per-row Activation Counters (RFM). DDR3 defense is OS / controller side via increased refresh rate, randomized address mapping, or ECC DIMMs.
fields.comparison_to_sibling_standards: DDR4 (JESD79-4) adds CRC on the data bus (optional, per BL8), parity on the command bus, and Target Row Refresh (TRR) hooks for Rowhammer mitigation. DDR5 (JESD79-5) adds on-die ECC, Refresh Management commands (RFM), and per-row Activation Counters. None of these protocol-level mitigations exist in DDR3.
fields.notes: Security at the DDR3 layer is intentionally absent in JEDEC's design. JESD79-3C is a high-throughput, low-cost, high-yield memory standard; security is the responsibility of the upstream memory controller / SoC. Modern systems that need at-rest DDR3 encryption use a memory controller with built-in AES (e.g., AMD Secure Memory Encryption SME) that encrypts/decrypts data transparently on the DDR3 channel without changing the DDR3 component spec.
